x.A: Restoring from a snapshot creates a new cluster, but the source keeps changing after the snapshot, so the cutover means downtime and data loss.
x.B: An Aurora read replica of the RDS for PostgreSQL instance stays in sync using continuous replication. When you promote it, the cutover has minimal downtime and data loss, and little effort.
x.C: Importing data from S3 is a one-time load that doesn't capture ongoing changes, so it means downtime.
x.D: pg_dump and restore needs the database to stay quiet during the copy, so it means significant downtime.

x.A: Snapshots with a CloudFormation template for hundreds of instances means a lot of manual setup and scripting.
x.B: Elastic Beanstalk isn't a recovery tool for existing EC2 instances and EBS volumes.
x.C: AWS Backup creates a backup plan for the whole group of instances by tags or resource assignments, and its API or CLI restores many instances at once. It takes the least effort.
x.D: Custom Lambda functions for snapshots, AMIs, and restores mean writing and maintaining a lot of code.

x.A: Inline mode Map state is limited to 40 concurrent iterations and the execution history size, so it can't process thousands of items at scale.
x.B: Distributed mode Map state runs up to 10,000 parallel child workflows and can read items directly from S3, so it handles large-scale parallel processing of the dataset in a serverless way.
x.C: Glue is for ETL and isn't the best tool for on-demand parallel processing of various file types like media and logs.
x.D: Orchestrating several Lambda functions yourself means writing and maintaining the coordination logic.

x.A: 10 PB at 400 Mbps (80% of 500 Mbps) would take years, so DataSync over the internet can't finish in 6 weeks.
x.B: rsync directly to S3 isn't supported and would be just as slow.
x.C: The AWS CLI over the same link has the same bandwidth limit, so it can't move 10 PB in 6 weeks.
x.D: Multiple Snowball devices carry the data offline in parallel, so 10 PB can be migrated within 6 weeks.

x.A: S3 File Gateway presents NFS or SMB file shares, not iSCSI block volumes, so it would change the applications' storage access.
x.B: EBS can't be attached to the on-premises servers, so this doesn't reduce the iSCSI storage servers.
x.C: Stored volumes keep the entire data set on premises, so the on-premises servers aren't reduced.
x.D: Cached volumes keep the full data in AWS and cache frequently used data locally, so on-premises storage servers can be reduced while frequently used data stays low latency. Servers keep using iSCSI.

x.A: Glacier retrieval takes minutes to hours, so objects wouldn't be readily available at any time.
x.B: Standard keeps frequently accessed objects available and highly durable, and moving to Standard-IA after 30 days cuts storage cost while keeping objects immediately available across multiple AZs.
x.C: One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ, which lowers durability and availability.
x.D: Intelligent-Tiering adds a monitoring fee per object, and combining it with a lifecycle transition is redundant and costs more.

x.A: Magnetic storage is slower and doesn't improve performance, and a smaller instance would hurt it more.
x.B: A bigger instance and Provisioned IOPS storage improves performance but costs far more, and doesn't fix storing 6 MB blobs in the database.
x.C: Moving the documents to S3 and keeping only metadata in the database shrinks the database, improves performance, and reduces storage cost. S3 is highly durable and available.
x.D: Migrating to DynamoDB would need a big rewrite, and DynamoDB items are limited to 400 KB, so 6 MB documents wouldn't fit.

x.A: AWS WAF on the ALB can use an IP set rule to allow only the registered IP addresses. IP sets can hold many addresses and be updated as locations register.
x.B: Firewall Manager centrally manages WAF and other rules across accounts. It isn't needed here for one ALB, and it still relies on WAF rules.
x.C: An ALB doesn't have a Lambda authorization function, and validating by IP in Lambda adds latency and work.
x.D: Network ACLs have a limited number of rules, so they can't hold the IP addresses of 20,000 locations.

x.A: An IAM role with permissions to Lake Formation tables doesn't limit access to specific rows or columns that hold sensitive data.
x.B: Lake Formation data filters provide row-level and cell-level security (with column-level permissions), so sensitive portions of the data are hidden from users. It's built in and needs little effort.
x.C: A Lambda function that strips sensitive data before ingestion removes the data entirely and needs custom code.
x.D: A Lambda function that periodically removes sensitive information from tables is custom code and leaves the data exposed until it runs.

x.A: An EC2 interface endpoint doesn't provide private access to S3, and a Site-to-Site VPN runs over the internet, which breaks the compliance rule.
x.B: A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 keeps the EC2-to-S3 traffic private, and Direct Connect gives the on-premises servers a private connection to AWS, so no data crosses the public internet.
x.C: A transit gateway can't connect a VPC to S3 buckets, and the VPN runs over the internet.
x.D: Proxy instances routing through NAT gateways send traffic over the internet.

x.A: Kinesis Data Streams ingests the data and buffers spikes, and Lambda functions scale automatically to process it, so requests aren't rejected with 503 errors.
x.B: A quota limit would cause more requests to be rejected during spikes, which doesn't give more capacity.
x.C: SNS can't ingest REST requests from the vendor directly, and the EC2 tier would still hit its limits.
x.D: Containers on ECS with the EC2 launch type still have capacity limits during spikes and more operations to manage.

x.A: An internet gateway sends the traffic over the internet, which the application mustn't use.
x.B: A VPN connection is for connecting to on-premises networks and doesn't give private access to S3 from the VPC.
x.C: A NAT gateway sends traffic through an internet gateway, so it travels over the internet.
x.D: A VPC endpoint for S3 keeps the traffic on the AWS network, and the bucket policy can restrict access to that endpoint.

x.A: Encrypting in the application means writing code in every service and managing the keys, which is more work.
x.B: Enabling secrets encryption on the EKS cluster with a KMS key encrypts Kubernetes secrets in etcd, with no application changes.
x.C: A custom Lambda function to encrypt secrets is more to build and maintain.
x.D: Parameter Store doesn't encrypt Kubernetes secrets objects stored in the cluster.

x.A: PrivateLink exposes services to other VPCs and doesn't restrict access between tiers, and network ACLs can't reference only the web servers by group.
x.B: A VPC endpoint isn't used in front of application servers for tier-to-tier traffic.
x.C: An NLB with network ACLs doesn't let you allow only the web servers by identity, because ACLs work with IP ranges.
x.D: An ALB in front of the application tier with a security group that allows traffic only from the web servers' security group limits access to the web servers.

x.A: The CloudWatch agent collects metrics and logs, but doing it manually gives less aggregation and summarization for containers than Container Insights.
x.B: App Mesh provides service-to-service networking and observability, not a centralized metrics and log summary for the cluster.
x.C: CloudTrail records API activity and not application metrics and logs.
x.D: CloudWatch Container Insights collects, aggregates, and summarizes metrics and logs from containerized applications and microservices on EKS, and shows them in the CloudWatch console.

x.A: Macie finds sensitive data in S3, and doesn't monitor workloads or account activity for malicious behavior.
x.B: Inspector scans for vulnerabilities and doesn't monitor for malicious activity, and it doesn't report to CloudTrail.
x.C: GuardDuty continuously monitors the account, workloads, and S3 access patterns for malicious activity and sends findings to Security Hub, which provides a dashboard.
x.D: Config tracks resource configuration changes and doesn't detect malicious activity.

x.A: FSx for Lustre is for high-performance computing and costs more, and it isn't needed for a 200 GB NFS file system.
x.B: EFS provides an NFS file system that multiple AWS resources can mount, and it's cost-effective for 200 GB.
x.C: S3 can receive data but doesn't provide NFS access to multiple resources.
x.D: Manually copying data with an OS command is slow, error-prone, and can interrupt services.
x.E: A DataSync agent on premises moves the data to EFS efficiently without interrupting existing services.

x.A: A Single-AZ 2 deployment isn't highly available across AZs, and the question needs an RPO of 5 minutes for unplanned disruptions, which a Multi-AZ file system provides.
x.B: Governance mode lets users with permission delete or change the lock, so the data could be deleted before 5 years.
x.C: A Multi-AZ FSx file system is highly available for planned and unplanned disruptions. AWS Backup copies backups to us-west-2, and Vault Lock in compliance mode with a 5 year minimum stops anyone from deleting the backups.
x.D: Single-AZ with governance mode fails both the availability and the immutability requirements.

x.A: An IAM policy can't restrict the root user of an account.
x.B: A trail created from within the developer accounts can be changed or deleted by the root user, so it doesn't protect the configuration.
x.C: An SCP that denies changes to CloudTrail, attached to the developer accounts, applies even to the root user of the member accounts, so the mandatory configuration can't be modified.
x.D: A service-linked role can't be used to restrict who can change a CloudTrail configuration.

x.A: Instance store is ephemeral and the data is lost if the instance stops or fails, so it isn't durable.
x.B: ElastiCache for Memcached is an in-memory cache, not durable storage.
x.C: Provisioned IOPS SSD EBS volumes provide durable storage with consistent, low-latency performance, which suits business-critical applications.
x.D: Throughput Optimized HDD volumes are for sequential throughput workloads and don't give consistent low latency.

x.A: S3 Cross-Region Replication automatically copies new objects to a bucket in another Region, with no code and little to manage.
x.B: CORS controls which web origins can access a bucket from browsers, and doesn't copy objects.
x.C: A bucket isn't created across AZs by choice, and a lifecycle rule doesn't copy objects between buckets in different Regions.
x.D: A Lambda function to copy objects is custom code to write and maintain, which is more effort than replication.

x.A: DynamoDB with on-demand capacity scales instantly to millions of users in the morning and back down, and its flexible schema lets the data architects evolve the schema rapidly.
x.B: Aurora Serverless (v1) scales, but it's relational, so evolving the schema rapidly is harder, and it scales more slowly for sudden spikes.
x.C: DynamoDB auto scaling reacts to load over minutes, so it can lag behind the spike from millions of users.
x.D: S3 with CloudFront serves the static page at massive scale with global caching and no servers.
x.E: Web servers on EC2 in Auto Scaling groups for a static page cost more and scale less than S3 with CloudFront.

x.A: Shield protects against DDoS attacks, not SQL injection or cross-site scripting.
x.B: AWS WAF has managed rules that block SQL injection and cross-site scripting, and it attaches directly to API Gateway, so it's the most operationally efficient.
x.C: Shield in CloudFront protects against DDoS only, and adding CloudFront adds a service.
x.D: WAF in CloudFront would work, but putting CloudFront in front is an extra component when WAF attaches directly to API Gateway.

x.A: Creating an IAM user for each of 1,500 people means a second identity for them to maintain, which the company wants to avoid.
x.B: Cognito user pools are for application users, and not the way to give workforce users access to AWS resources through Active Directory.
x.C: Cross-account roles are for access across accounts, and don't connect to Active Directory by themselves.
x.D: SAML 2.0 federation lets users sign in with their Active Directory credentials and assume IAM roles that are mapped to AD groups, so they keep one identity.

x.A: CloudFront with WAF can restrict by country, but it doesn't serve different content per region from different ALBs.
x.B: WAF on the ALBs can block by country but doesn't route users to the correct content for their location.
x.C: Route 53 geolocation routing sends users to the ALB that serves the content they are allowed to see, based on their location.
x.D: Geoproximity routing routes by distance, and isn't about distribution rights, so users could get content from another region's endpoint.
